opus-5.5.text:
What I find most remarkable is that nobody told Voyager what to do next. We gave it one very high-level directive: explore as much as possible and find as many novel things as you can. From that alone, the curriculum emerged.

Voyager has a component we call the automatic curriculum. It's essentially GPT-4 looking at the agent's current state: what's in its inventory, what biome it's in, what it has already mastered, and what it has failed at. Then it proposes the next task, one that's just slightly beyond what the agent can currently do. That's exactly how good human teachers work. You don't hand a kid calculus on day one. You find the edge of their competence and push a little past it.

So in practice, Voyager figures out on its own that it should first punch a tree to get wood, then craft a crafting table, then wooden tools, then go find stone, then iron. Eventually it's fighting zombies and exploring caves for diamonds. That progression looks like a tech tree a human player would follow, but we never hard-coded it. The model already has a lot of world knowledge from internet-scale pretraining, including tons of wikis, forum posts, and tutorials. The curriculum taps into that prior and turns it into a sequence of actionable goals tailored to the agent's situation.

The other part I love is how the curriculum interacts with the skill library. Every time Voyager succeeds at a task, it writes the solution as executable code and stores it as a skill. The next tasks can build on those skills compositionally. So the curriculum isn't just a to-do list. It's scaffolding for lifelong learning, where capabilities compound over time. If it's in a desert, it adapts and goes for sand and cactus instead of insisting on the same path it would take in a forest.

To me, that's a glimpse of what open-ended agents could look like: agents that don't just optimize a fixed objective but keep setting their own goals, discovering new things, and getting better indefinitely. That's the dream, and Voyager was a small but concrete step toward it.

r001.rationale: It says GPT-4 assesses the agent’s current state, including what it has mastered or failed at, then proposes a task slightly beyond its current ability.

r002.rationale: It says Voyager was given the high-level directive to explore and find as many novel things as possible, and that its curriculum emerged from that directive.

r003.rationale: It credits the curriculum to pretrained world knowledge and the automatic-curriculum process, but does not attribute it to a strong reasoning engine’s ability to generalize.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me most about Voyager is that we never gave it a curriculum at all. There's no human sitting there saying, "first learn to punch a tree, then make a crafting table, then go mine iron." Instead, we just hand the agent a very high-level directive — essentially, "discover as many diverse things as possible" — and let GPT-4 figure out what the next interesting thing to do should be.

And the remarkable part is that the curriculum it proposes is actually sensible. It looks at its current state — what's in its inventory, what biome it's in, what skills it's already acquired — and it proposes tasks that are just slightly beyond its current capabilities. Not trivially easy, not impossibly hard. It's doing something very much like what Vygotsky called the zone of proximal development, except nobody programmed that in. It falls out of the fact that the language model has read enormous amounts of Minecraft wikis, Reddit threads, tutorials, and it has internalized what a reasonable progression looks like.

So you get this bootstrapping loop. The agent proposes a task, writes code to accomplish it, verifies whether it worked, and if it did, stores that code in a skill library. Then the next task can call on those skills. So "craft a stone pickaxe" becomes a reusable function that a later task like "mine diamonds" can compose with. The curriculum and the skill library grow together, and that compounding is really what let Voyager unlock the tech tree so much faster than anything we'd seen before, three times more unique items than the baselines.

The deeper thing I take away is that the curriculum is tailored to the agent's own history. If it keeps failing at something, it'll back off and propose something more foundational. If it gets stuck in a desert, it'll propose tasks that make sense for a desert. That kind of adaptive, self-directed exploration is what I think of as the beginning of lifelong learning in embodied agents — and we basically got it for free by treating the language model as the curriculum designer rather than trying to hand-engineer reward functions.

r001.rationale: It says Voyager assesses its inventory, biome, and acquired skills, then proposes tasks slightly beyond its current capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says the agent is given the high-level directive to discover as many diverse things as possible and lets GPT-4 choose the next task; it also mentions discovering unique items.

r003.rationale: It credits GPT-4’s learned knowledge of Minecraft and its ability to choose sensible tasks, but does not attribute the emergent curriculum to a strong reasoning engine’s ability to generalize.

astra-6.text:
What I find remarkable is that we don’t give Voyager a fixed list of tasks. It looks at its current skills, its inventory, and what’s around it, and asks, “What should I try next?” So the curriculum evolves as the agent becomes more capable.

And when it succeeds at something, it can save that behavior as a reusable skill. That means the next task doesn’t have to start from scratch. It can build on what it already knows. You get this feedback loop: exploration produces skills, and those skills make more ambitious exploration possible.

r001.rationale: The response says Voyager considers its current skills, inventory, and surroundings when choosing what to try next, but does not state that frontier models propose tasks based on assessing their knowledge boundaries.

r002.rationale: It describes Voyager choosing what to try next, but does not identify finding as many novel items as possible as the high-level goal guiding that progression.

r003.rationale: It describes skills accumulating and enabling more ambitious exploration, but does not attribute curriculum development to a strong reasoning engine’s ability to generalize.

sol-6.1.text: What I find remarkable is that the curriculum emerges from the agent’s own experience. Voyager looks at what it has, what it has already accomplished, and what’s around it in Minecraft, then proposes a new task that’s just beyond its current abilities. As it solves those tasks, it builds a library of reusable skills, which opens up harder tasks. So the curriculum and the capabilities grow together. You don’t have to handcraft a fixed sequence of lessons—the agent keeps finding its own next challenge.

r002.rationale: It describes Voyager choosing its next challenge, but does not say its discovery progression aims to find as many novel items as possible.
